title: A job scheduler
description:
An operating system decides which waiting job runs next on the processor. Build a simulator that compares three classic **scheduling policies**, using sorting to process jobs in order of arrival and a **priority queue** to pick the next job to run. The program reads one command per line until the end of the input: ``` job build 0 3 2 job hotfix 2 1 9 job tests 1 4 5 job docs 9 2 1 run priority compare ``` prints ``` added build added hotfix added tests added docs run priority 0-3 build (waited 0) 3-4 hotfix (waited 1) 4-8 tests (waited 3) 8-9 idle 9-11 docs (waited 0) average wait 1.00, longest wait 3 (tests), finished at 11 priority: average wait 1.00, finished at 11 shortest: average wait 1.00, finished at 11 fifo: average wait 1.75, finished at 11 best: priority ``` **Jobs**: `job ` adds a job and prints `added `. The arrival is a whole number from 0, the duration from 1, the priority from 1 to 9 (9 is the most urgent); all three at most 1000000. A line that does not fit prints `error: usage: job `, and a name already in use prints `error: job already exists`. **The simulation** has one processor and never interrupts a running job. Whenever the processor is free at time `t`, it chooses among the jobs that have arrived (`arrival <= t`) and not yet run: | Policy | Chooses | Ties broken by | |---|---|---| | `fifo` | the earliest arrival | name (alphabetical) | | `priority` | the highest priority | earliest arrival, then name | | `shortest` | the shortest duration | earliest arrival, then name | Names compare the way `std::string` does, character code by character code, so capital letters come before small ones (`lateR` before `later`). If no job has arrived yet, the processor is idle until the next arrival. A job's **wait** is its start time minus its arrival. Every run starts at time 0. **Commands**: | Command | Output | |---|---| | `run ` | `run `, then a line ` - (waited )` per job in the order they run, and ` - idle` for every idle gap; then `average wait , longest wait (), finished at `, with the average to two decimals and the name of the first job that waited longest. With no jobs: `nothing to run` | | `compare` | For each policy, `: average wait , finished at `, ordered by average wait (lowest first; ties in the order fifo, priority, shortest), then `best: ` for the first line. With no jobs: `nothing to run` | | `jobs` | Each job as ` arrives , takes , priority

`, sorted by arrival then name; or `no jobs` | | `remove ` | `removed `, or `error: no job ` | An unknown policy prints `error: policy must be fifo, priority or shortest`; a known command with the wrong number of words prints `error: usage: run ` (or `compare`, `jobs`, `remove `); anything else prints `error: unknown command ''`. Blank lines are ignored.
hints: `std::priority_queue` keeps the element that is largest by its comparator on top. If `runsBefore(a, b)` says a should run first, give the queue the reverse, `[](a, b) { return runsBefore(b, a); }`, so the job that runs first counts as the largest.

`std::tie(a.arrival, a.name) < std::tie(b.arrival, b.name)` compares by arrival and then by name. For "highest priority first", compare `-a.priority` with `-b.priority` (with `std::make_tuple`, since `std::tie` needs variables).
requirements: Sort the jobs by arrival time once per run (`std::sort` with a comparator), then sweep through them with an index, moving each arrived job into the ready queue.
Keep the ready jobs in a `std::priority_queue` (or your heap from practice 3.04) whose comparator implements the policy: each run is O(n log n).
Use `std::stable_sort` to order the policies in `compare`.
A `Job` struct, a `RunResult` struct holding the timeline and the statistics, and a `simulate(jobs, policy)` function that does no printing.
stretch: Add a **preemptive** `shortest-remaining` policy: when a job arrives whose duration is shorter than the remaining time of the running one, the running job goes back into the queue. Print each slice of a job separately.
rules: Choose the next job with a priority queue.
